title: Europe’s lost reason of state
gist: Jack Dickens argues Europe has lost the doctrine of reason of state that Adenauer invoked over Suez in 1956, with legal process — epitomised by the European Court of Human Rights — displacing any definition of strategic ends, leaving the continent unable to act on migration, Ukraine or the Middle East despite being the most exposed party in each.

themes.theme: Reason of state as lost European doctrine

insights.claim: Konrad Adenauer backed the 1956 Franco-British-Israeli seizure of the Suez canal zone and called it an act of European reason of state, treating Europe as a commonwealth with its own distinct strategic and economic interests.
insights.speaker: Jack Dickens
insights.so_what: The precedent an emerging European strategic-autonomy caucus can cite: continental interests can justify force independent of Washington.
insights.locator: Konrad Adenauer is not a figure usually

insights.claim: Machiavelli's Discourses (Book III, Chapter 41) is the origin of the doctrine that when a country's survival is at stake, considerations of justice, mercy or shame must not constrain the statesman.
insights.speaker: Jack Dickens
insights.so_what: The intellectual licence for European hard-power decisions is being openly re-argued from first principles — a leading indicator of policy loosening.
insights.quote: where the ultimate decision concerning the safety of one’s country is to be taken, no consideration of what is just or unjust, merciful or cruel, praiseworthy or shameful should be permitted
insights.locator: Reason of state was forged as an idea

insights.claim: The core European failure is not a lack of capability but a lack of defined strategic ends, with legal and procedural process substituted for the choice of objectives.
insights.speaker: Jack Dickens
insights.so_what: Expect European defence and migration policy to stay reactive until ends are named — capability spending without doctrine converts poorly into deterrence.
insights.quote: The lawfare state has for too long triumphed over the warfare state.
insights.locator: European countries, and the European community

insights.claim: Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen argued at the 2025 Munich Security Conference that European states are too enamoured with process and must first identify strategic ends and then will the means.
insights.speaker: Jack Dickens
insights.so_what: A sitting EU head of government voicing the ends-before-means critique marks where the political centre of gravity on European rearmament is heading.
insights.locator: The current Danish Prime Minister, Mette Frederiksen

themes.theme: Europe's asymmetric exposure to the periphery

insights.claim: Europe was disproportionately hit by Nasser's 1956 nationalisation of the Suez Canal because it was far more dependent than the United States on oil and trade transiting the canal zone, and far more geopolitically exposed to the southern Mediterranean.
insights.speaker: Jack Dickens
insights.so_what: The structural asymmetry persists: chokepoint and Middle East disruptions transmit to European energy and freight costs before American ones.

insights.claim: European countries are simultaneously the most exposed to the economic fallout from rising energy prices out of the Middle East and the least able to shape the region's conflicts.
insights.speaker: Jack Dickens
insights.so_what: Prices in European energy and its industrial complex carry a geopolitical risk premium that Europe itself cannot hedge by influence — only by supply diversification.
insights.locator: In the Middle East, European countries are most exposed

insights.claim: Europe's capitals have improvised their support for Ukraine without defining what victory looks like, and without any notion of how it could be achieved absent continued American support.
insights.speaker: Jack Dickens
insights.so_what: Any scenario that removes US backing exposes the absence of a European war aim — a tail risk for defence procurement timelines and Ukraine-linked reconstruction assumptions.
insights.locator: Europe’s capitals have fumbled their way

themes.theme: Rights, courts and the common good

insights.claim: Rights adjudication has produced a self-defeating imbalance in which individual legal entitlements routinely override the common good, with deportation policy bound up in legal challenges on what the author calls spurious human-rights grounds.
insights.speaker: Jack Dickens
insights.so_what: Legal-institutional reform of migration enforcement is becoming mainstream European commentary — watch for treaty-level challenges to ECHR jurisdiction.
insights.locator: At home, illegal immigration tests the continent’s borders

insights.claim: The European Court of Human Rights is singled out as the institution that most embodies the elevation of abstract legal right over the wellbeing of the political community.
insights.speaker: Jack Dickens
insights.so_what: Named-institution criticism from establishment-adjacent outlets precedes political attempts at derogation or withdrawal — a live European legal risk.

insights.claim: The critique is not anti-rights: natural rights are presented as a genuine part of Europe's civilisational heritage dating to the jurists and philosophers of medieval universities, with the problem located in activist judges treating rights as a supreme good in themselves.
insights.speaker: Jack Dickens
insights.so_what: Distinguishes the reformist European right from the abolitionist one — the likelier policy path is reinterpretation, not repudiation.
insights.locator: The idea of natural rights has a long and rich history

insights.claim: Donald Tusk framed Europe's defence paradox as 500 million Europeans asking 300 million Americans to defend them against 140 million Russians.
insights.speaker: Jack Dickens
insights.so_what: The demographic arithmetic is the standard rhetorical lever for US burden-shifting demands — it argues for sustained European defence budget growth.
insights.quote: 500 million Europeans are asking 300 million Americans to defend them against 140 million Russians

insights.claim: The deeper constraint on European strategy is culture and electoral incentives rather than philosophy: democratic leaders are responding accurately to voters who simply do not care about defence.
insights.speaker: Jack Dickens
insights.so_what: Implies European rearmament is fragile and reversible once headlines fade — favour contracted, multi-year defence programmes over sentiment-driven exposure.
insights.locator: This is a problem of culture and incentives
